The core evidence remains: (1) ultrasound identified a *cystic mass*, (2) it is associated with *dilated bile ducts* and *extrahepatic biliary obstruction*, (3) clinical presentation includes *painless jaundice* and *rapid weight loss*, (4) urgent workup centers on *cyst characterization* (EUS-FNA + cyst fluid analysis), not solid-mass biopsy — strongly implying the lesion’s cystic nature is radiologically established and clinically decisive. Among cystic pancreaticobiliary neoplasms, IPMN is the most common cause of painless obstructive jaundice with a cystic-appearing head lesion — especially when ductal communication is suspected (hence MRCP priority). Distal cholangiocarcinoma is typically *stricturing*, not cystic; cystic degeneration is rare and usually incidental, not dominant. Ampullary tumors may rarely appear cystic but more commonly present as polypoid or solid masses. The emphasis on *duct–cyst communication*, *cyst fluid CEA/amylase*, and *KRAS/GNAS* testing — all canonical for IPMN evaluation — further anchors this diagnosis. No other cystic lesion has this precise diagnostic workflow.
